Breathing: what to do and when

When you are stressed, your body reacts on its own: the heart beats faster and breathing gets shallow. Breathing is one of the few parts of this you can control directly. Many studies show that slow breathing, at about 6 breaths a minute, calms the body: the heartbeat settles into a calmer, more flexible rhythm (researchers measure this as heart rate variability).

Well researched

Whether it raises your score is much less clear. Small studies with sport shooters and one study with police pistol shooters found it helped, but we found no study in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting.

Little research

  1. Training days: 5–10 minutes of slow breathing at about 6 breaths a minute, for example in for 4 seconds and out for 6.
  2. 2–5 minutes before the stand: 6–10 slow breaths, with a longer breath out if that feels comfortable.
  3. In the routine, just before the call: one natural breath out and loose shoulders, then the call.
  4. After a lost target: one slow breath out as the signal to reset.

Coaches' experience

If you practise slow breathing on ordinary days, your body learns to calm down faster, so on competition day it may come more easily. A heart-rate sensor that shows your heart rhythm live (this is called biofeedback) can help, but you do not need one.

Some research

Before the stand there is no time pressure, so a few slow breaths can lower tension without getting in the way. In Compak® Sporting, if your squad has six shooters, the wait behind station 1 is a good moment (Chapter 17 · Squad rotation through the stations).

Coaches' experience

Just before the call, keep the breath short and natural. In one lab study, slow paced breathing slowed reaction time. Clay shooting starts with a reaction to the target, and the delay after the call is often hard to predict (in Sporting™, and in Compak® Sporting with a manual release). So one easy breath out is enough here.

Little research

After a miss, one slow breath out can mark the end of that target. It works as a reset signal: see Reset after a miss.

Coaches' experience

You may hear of box breathing: in, hold, out and hold, four counts each. It is one option you can try. When researchers compared it with other ways of breathing, it did no better; in one study, simply breathing out longer than you breathe in worked better.

Little research

The “physiological sigh” is two breaths in through the nose and one long breath out. In one study, five minutes a day of it improved mood. We found no study of it just before a shot.

Little research

Many people find a breath out that is longer than the breath in relaxing. Studies disagree on whether it adds anything, so choose the rhythm that feels comfortable.

Little research

Safety: Breathing exercises should feel easy. If you feel dizzy or short of breath, return to normal breathing. If you have a heart or lung condition, ask your doctor first.

Key points

  • Slow breathing calms the body; you can practise it 5–10 minutes on training days.
  • Before the stand: a few slow breaths, with a comfortable longer breath out.
  • At the call: one natural breath out and loose shoulders, not long slow breathing.
  • After a miss: one slow breath out to start the reset.
  • Box breathing and the physiological sigh are options to try; research on them is limited.

Did you know?

Slow breathing at about 6 breaths a minute is sometimes called resonance breathing: at this pace, heart rate and breathing tend to rise and fall together.

For the coach
  • Teach slow breathing away from the stand, on training days. On the stand, keep only the short natural breath out before the call.

Terms

  • Pre-shot routine
  • Call
  • Box breathing

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. What can you try just before the call?

    1. Ten slow breaths at six a minute
    2. One natural breath out, shoulders down
    3. Holding your breath for a count of four
    Answer

    One natural breath out, shoulders down

    Long, slow breathing right before the call may slow your reaction; keep slow breaths for before the stand.

  2. What does research say about box breathing?

    1. It works clearly better than other methods
    2. It is not allowed in competitions
    3. It is one option, with little research
    Answer

    It is one option, with little research

    When researchers compared box breathing with other ways of breathing, it was not better; you can try it, but it is not a sure fix.

  3. When is slow breathing at about six breaths a minute a good fit?

    1. On training days and before the stand
    2. Right up to the very moment of the call
    3. Only after the whole round is over
    Answer

    On training days and before the stand

    Use slow breathing when there is no time pressure; at the call, one natural breath out is enough.
